thread:
Customer SRE (Acme): Hey team — since moving our customer-managed Envoy gateway into the VPC we’re seeing short bursts of 429s against the Redwood Private endpoint. Traffic pattern: sudden fan-out from Lambda-style workers, lasts ~20-40s then goes back to normal. No quota changes on our side. Anyone seen this pattern?
Alex P.: Thanks for flagging — does the 429 come from your gateway (Envoy/nginx) or from Redwood’s control plane? Can you paste a raw response header or a small log line?
Customer SRE (Acme):  Here’s a snippet from our envoy access log (redacted):

"2026-02-27T15:12:03Z 10.10.2.5:43212 - \"POST /v1/generate HTTP/1.1\" 429 - 0 125 12 9 \"-\" \"okhttp/4.9.0\""

And this is a sample response body we see in the client: 

{
  "error": "rate_limit_exceeded",
  "detail": "local_rate_limit"
}

We also see envoy stat: 

"http.local_rate_limit.filter_disabled: 0"
"http.local_rate_limit.enforced: 314"

Customer SRE (Acme): So looks like envoy is enforcing a local ratelimit. We did wire up the local_rate_limit filter to protect downstreams — but not sure what the right threshold is for bursty workloads hitting Redwood.
Maya S.: @Customer SRE (Acme) thanks. Two quick clarifying Qs: 1) Is your gateway using Envoy’s local_rate_limit (local) or a global rate limit service (RLS) with Redis/async backend? 2) Are you preserving the original client IP in x-forwarded-for so the limit keys are per-client?
Customer SRE (Acme): We’re using Envoy local rate limit (local). x-forwarded-for is preserved. We did not wire an external RLS yet.
Alex P.: That explains it. Envoy local_rate_limit is token-bucket-y but is local to each proxy instance. Under fan-out you can easily exhaust tokens on the node that receives the burst. If you have many pods behind a K8s Service some pods will be hit harder depending on kube-proxy balancing.
Devon R.: Quick triage checklist:
- Check which component returns 429: envoy or upstream. The log you pasted shows envoy returning the 429 (local_rate_limit).
- Inspect Envoy config for local_rate_limit settings (token_count, fill_interval, unit).
- Check ingress controller (nginx/traefik) annotations if you’re using them in front of Envoy.

Alex P.: Can you run these repro steps so we get concrete numbers?
1) From a bastion inside the VPC run: 
```bash
hey -n 2000 -c 200 -z 20s -H \"Authorization: Bearer <token>\" https://<envoy-gw-host>/v1/generate
```
2) On the envoy pod: `kubectl logs -n gateway <envoy-pod> | grep local_rate_limit`
3) Get envoy stats: `kubectl exec -n gateway <envoy-pod> -- curl -s localhost:9901/stats | grep local_rate_limit`

Customer SRE (Acme): Running now. I see a spike in `http.local_rate_limit.enforced` and the client sees ~18% 429s during the burst.
Maya S.: Ok. Short-term mitigations:
- Increase local_rate_limit tokens and/or the fill interval window so that tokens cover expected burst amplitude. e.g. if token_count = 100 in a 1s window, bump to 1000 for gateway nodes that should absorb bursts.
- Add an external rate limit service (RLS) so you get a centralized quota instead of per-proxy local buckets. We can share example Envoy + RLS configs.
- Configure front proxy to spread traffic more evenly (serviceAffinity, sessionAffinity off, or external LB to do round-robin).

Devon R.: For Kubernetes-specific knobs:
- Check ingress controller pod count and HPA: if you only have 2 ingress/ENVOY pods you’ll saturate them on burst. Scale to handle p95 burst concurrency.
- Verify kube-proxy mode (iptables vs ipvs). ipvs has better distribution for high-concurrency.
- Node-level conntrack and nf_conntrack_max can be a bottleneck. `ss -s` and `cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max` are useful.

Alex P.: Example Envoy local_rate_limit config we recommend (tuned for short bursts):
```yaml
filters:
- name: envoy.filters.http.local_ratelimit
  typed_config:
    "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.local_ratelimit.v3.LocalRateLimit
    stat_prefix: local_rate_limit
    token_bucket:
      max_tokens: 2000     # increase to absorb short bursts
      tokens_per_fill: 2000
      fill_interval: 1s
    filter_enabled:
      runtime_key: local_rate_limit_enabled
      default_value:
        numerator: 100
        denominator: HUNDRED
    filter_enforced:
      runtime_key: local_rate_limit_enforced
      default_value:
        numerator: 100
        denominator: HUNDRED
```

Customer SRE (Acme): Is it safe to set token_bucket.max_tokens very high? worried about accidental DoS if a client actually keeps sending.
Maya S.: Good question. Local rate limit is only protecting the local proxy process — raising tokens allows the node to accept bigger bursts but doesn’t create global fairness. If you want global fairness + per-API quotas, use external RLS backed by Redis (or our gateway if you want centralized limits). Alternatively combine: local_rate_limit with a smaller global limit at the RLS.

Devon R.: Operational checklist for a diagnostic run:
- Run the `hey` repro to reproduce and capture envoy stats pre/during/post.
- `kubectl get pods -n gateway -o wide` to see how many nodes/pods and which nodes are handling traffic.
- `kubectl top pods -n gateway` to check CPU spikes causing slow processing (which can increase apparent concurrency).
- If using nginx ingress in front of Envoy, check nginx annotations like `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-connections` and `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps` which might be triggering at 429 as well.

Customer SRE (Acme): We do have an nginx ingress in front of envoy (legacy). Migration missed that — nginx had `limit-rps: 100` and `limit-connections: 50`. Maybe that’s the real choke.
Alex P.: Bingo. If nginx in front is limiting, envoy’s local_rate_limit is just an additional layer. You’ll want to remove/relax the nginx annotations if you rely on envoy or centralized RLS.

Maya S.: Also FYI, when sending traffic to Redwood Private endpoints you should preserve the `x-request-id` and `x-forwarded-for` headers so we can correlate logs if you open a support ticket. If you want us to look we’ll need: the bastion repro command, envoy stats, and one sample request/response pair including headers.

Customer SRE (Acme): Copy. I’ll relax nginx limits, bump envoy tokens, and re-run the test. I’ll paste logs if any 429s remain.

Ops Bot: :ticket: Support ticket #RWD-4581 created and attached to this thread. Please add the logs to the ticket when ready.

Alex P.: TL;DR recommendations:
- Short term: relax/remove nginx ingress annotations that limit rps/connections, increase envoy local_rate_limit tokens to cover expected burst, and scale ingress/envoy pods.
- Mid term: deploy an external RLS (Redis-backed) for centralized quotas or use Redwood’s dedicated quota controls if you want provider-side centralized enforcement.
- When you re-run, attach envoy admin stats + one raw client request/response with headers to the ticket so we can confirm the 429 source.

Customer SRE (Acme): Thanks all — initial change looks good, 429s dropped from 18% to ~1% during the same synthetic burst. Will keep monitoring and follow up in the ticket with finalized config.

Maya S.: Awesome — ping us if anything persists and we’ll jump in for a live debug. :thumbsup:
